record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: What physical mechanism produces the large-scale magnetic fields observed in about 5% to 10% of early-type main-sequence stars? In particular, do stellar mergers create the stable large-scale toroidal-poloidal magnetic topologies needed for long-term fields, or do only some mergers do so, and could the observed field incidence instead be limited by magnetic-field decay on a timescale comparable to the main-sequence lifetime?

evidence.quote: 2.2. What causes large scale magnetic fields in stars?
However, further work is needed to verify this idea. The number of slow rotators amongst early B type stars, for example, seems clearly larger than the number of magnetic early B stars.
Alternatively, Fossati et al. (2016) suggested that large scale magnetic fields in massive stars may decay on a timescale comparable to their main sequence lifetime.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Approximately 5%–10% of early-type main-sequence stars (spectral types O, B, and A) are observed to host detectable large-scale, ordered surface magnetic fields with stable mixed toroidal–poloidal topologies, while the remaining majority show no such fields at current detection limits. Identify the physical mechanism responsible for the production and long-term stability of these large-scale magnetic fields. In particular, address the following:

(a) Can the coalescence (merger) of two stars during the pre-main-sequence or main-sequence phase generically produce a stable, large-scale toroidal–poloidal magnetic configuration that survives on stellar evolutionary timescales, and if so, what fraction of mergers do so?

(b) If only a subset of mergers produces such configurations, what physical parameters of the progenitor binary (mass ratio, evolutionary stage at coalescence, rotation, initial magnetic state) determine whether a stable large-scale field is generated?

(c) Could the observed incidence of magnetic early-type stars be limited not by the rarity of the field-generating event but by Ohmic or topological decay of the large-scale field on a timescale comparable to the main-sequence lifetime, and what observational and theoretical tests can distinguish this scenario from a merger origin?
artifact.status_search_result: The question remains open. Recent works pursue both hypotheses: 3D MHD simulations of massive-star mergers (Schneider et al. 2019, Nature; and follow-up simulations in 2025) show mergers can generate strong fields and account for roughly the observed ~10% incidence, while Fossati et al. (2016) and subsequent analyses present evidence consistent with field decay on the main-sequence timescale. No consensus mechanism has been established, and ongoing simulation and observational programs continue to test the merger versus decay scenarios.

status_evidence.claim: Merger hypothesis remains a leading but unconfirmed scenario.

status_evidence.title: Evidence of magnetic field decay in massive main-sequence stars
status_evidence.snippet: Magnetic fields may decay on a timescale of the order of the main-sequence lifetime.
status_evidence.claim: Field-decay scenario is an active competing hypothesis.

status_evidence.title: Magnetic field generation in mergers of massive main sequence stars
status_evidence.snippet: Recent MHD simulations of massive-star mergers explore field generation.
status_evidence.claim: Active 2025 research continues to test the merger origin, indicating the question is unresolved.
